title: Ogre Holl and the Flow of Time
markdown:
The sun, a magnificent artist, was painting the sky with pink and gold over the very highest peaks of the Whispering Mountains. For Ogre Holl, this was no ordinary morning. He was a very big ogre, and even more importantly, he was very earnest. Today was the day he would journey to meet Elder Gristle. Elder Gristle was a wise old ogre whose words were said to sound like falling rocks and whose ideas were as clear as melted ice.

"Now then, Moss, my most loyal and fluffy friend!" boomed Holl, his voice a delightful rumble that might shake teacups from distant shelves. He smoothed his roughspun tunic, giving a decisive tug to the neatly folded napkin peeking from his collar. "Today, my dear fellow, we shall make a most splendid impression! I have rehearsed my magnificent opening address a staggering, nay, a glorious, seventeen times!"

Moss, a ram of magnificent fleece and unshakeable devotion, responded with a soft, resonant "Baaaaa" from his usual spot near Holl’s huge, muddy boots. It was a bleat that spoke volumes, suggesting perhaps that seventeen speeches were quite enough for one morning, and a good scratch behind the horns was a far more pressing matter.

Holl, possessed of a politeness that belied his ogre size, chuckled and obliged. "Ah, indeed, a most clever thought, my dear Moss! A treat for the soul, and for the stomach, must come before any grand declarations!" With surprising gentleness, he produced an apple of truly heroic proportions, polished to a mirror-like gleam, and presented it to his ram with a flourish.

And so, the adventure began, a magnificent unfolding of trails and triumphs. They ambled through orchards so laden with fruit, the branches bowed low as if in greeting. The air was thick with the intoxicating perfume of ripening apples, a sweet contrast to the bracing, crisp mountain air. They passed by the stoic ruins of ancient watchtowers, their stones worn smooth by countless seasons of wind and rain. Holl, with a glint in his eye, imagined the brave sentinels who had once scanned these very horizons, their hearts as stout as the granite beneath their feet.

"And so, most esteemed Elder Gristle," Holl practiced, his voice echoing with a theatrical boom across a sun-dappled meadow, "I have journeyed forth from the green valley, yearning to bask in the bright glow of your deep wisdom, eager to learn all you know!" He puffed out his chest, feeling quite pleased with the grand sound of his words.

Moss, meanwhile, let out a quiet, but clear, "Baaa." To Holl’s sharp ears, it sounded remarkably like an announcement that a particularly juicy patch of wild mountain thyme beckoned just beyond a cluster of moss-covered boulders. Ever attentive to his faithful companion's needs, Holl graciously steered their course, allowing Moss a moment of tasty delight.

As the sky began its slow, majestic transformation into hues of deep violet and hushed indigo, signaling the approach of twilight, they arrived at "The Gilded Goblet." This inn, a place of loud fun and a bit wobbly walls, was nestled cozily in a sheltered gorge, its very existence seeming to ward off the mountain's chill. A sign, painted with a charm that far outweighed its artistry, proudly proclaimed its name. Inside, the air was a delightful mix of the savory scent of roasted root vegetables and the merry clamor of cheerful patrons. Presiding over this busy, happy mess was Fizzwick, the goblin innkeeper, a creature always busy, with eyes as sharp as dark glass.

"Well met, well met, welcome travelers!" Fizzwick chirped, his voice a bright, clear sound that cut through the din. "Holl the Hearty, and your fancy sheep friend! Come in, come in! The finest mountain stew is bubbling merrily, and our cider, I assure you, is the best made this year!"

Holl beamed, a warm wave of confidence washing over him. He requested a modest, yet hearty, portion of stew for himself, and a generous mound of the freshest greens for Moss. He straightened his napkin once more, feeling the moment was ripe for some smart thinking. "Fizzwick, my good sir," he began, leaning in conspiratorially, his voice dropping to a more intimate tone, "I must confess, I have been diligently practicing my address to Elder Gristle. It involves a clever comparison, you see, about how time always moves forward."

Just as the words left Holl’s lips, a harsh, grating caw ripped through the cozy atmosphere from the rafters above. A large, magnificent raven, its feathers glossy black and its eyes like tiny, intelligent beads, ruffled its plumage and fixed its gaze upon Holl. A peculiar stillness descended upon the immediate vicinity.

The raven cawed again, a sound that sent a shiver down Holl's massive spine. "Flow of time!" it croaked, in a voice that was a startlingly accurate, yet rather mischievous, echo of Holl’s own, tinged with a peculiar raspy edge.

Holl froze, his enormous green cheeks flushing a bright, mortified crimson. "Oh, goodness me," he murmured, a wave of embarrassment washing over him. He had completely forgotten that he had been muttering his practice phrases aloud while trekking through the wilderness.

Fizzwick, a goblin who had seen more than his fair share of peculiar happenings within the walls of "The Gilded Goblet," merely raised a single, expressive eyebrow. "A remarkably eloquent bird you seem to have acquired, Holl," he remarked with a sly grin.

"He… he tends to repeat things," Holl explained, his voice strained. "Only one particular phrase, mind you. A rather unfortunate utterance I let slip by accident earlier on the path."

The raven, sensing it had a captivated audience, let out another dramatic, attention-grabbing squawk. "Flow of time!" it shrieked, its voice sounding so much like his, it was spooky.

Holl slumped slightly, his big plans suddenly feeling flat. This was certainly not the good start he had hoped for. He attempted to steer the conversation towards safer, more ordinary topics, but each effort was met with the raven's constant, repeating cry. "The finest apples in the northern territories are said to grow in this very region!" Holl might venture, only to be answered by the distinct, unnerving cry of, "Flow of time!"

The following morning dawned with an amazing sight. As the first rays of dawn, like molten gold paint, spilled over the tall, snowy mountains, a vast shadow fell across the inn's doorway. Elder Gristle stood silhouetted against the brilliant light, his immense, ancient form radiating an aura of quiet, immeasurable power. He had arrived.

Holl's heart began to hammer against his ribs like a runaway boulder. He rose to his feet, attempting to summon the courage and eloquence for his practiced greeting. "Esteemed Elder Gristle," he began, his voice trembling with a mixture of awe and apprehension, "I have journeyed forth from the green valley to bask in the bright glow of your deep wisdom…"

"Flow of time!" shrieked the raven, Reginald, as he was now known, who had evidently taken up a prime perch on a sturdy beam directly above Elder Gristle's old, respected head.

Holl winced, his big shoulders slumping. He could not, in good conscience, continue. Fizzwick, ever the accommodating host, scurried to offer Elder Gristle a comfortable seat and a steaming mug of potent, dark brew.

Elder Gristle, however, did not display even a sign of annoyance. Instead, he seemed to be very amused. He watched the raven, Reginald, with a twinkle in his old, wrinkled eyes. "Ah, Reginald, my old friend," he rumbled, his voice a deep, comforting bass that seemed to resonate with the very earth. "Still indulging your love of making big speeches, I see."

Holl blinked, utterly bewildered. "You… you know the raven, Elder?"

"Reginald and I have shared many seasons," Elder Gristle replied, taking a slow, contemplative sip of his drink. "He has a rather peculiar habit of repeating phrases, you see. Especially those that tend to introduce a bit of gentle, good-natured chaos. He once kept me laughing for two weeks by complaining loudly about lost glasses."

Holl stared, his ogre brain slowly figuring out what was happening. Then, a dawning realization, warm and bright, spread across his face. Elder Gristle was not judging him for the raven's disruptive commentary. He was understanding. He was amused.

"It would appear," Elder Gristle continued, a kindly smile spreading across his craggy features like sunlight over a mountain range, "that the real test of wisdom isn't giving perfect speeches. It's about how you handle the unexpected squawks and happy chirps of life. For you see, dear Holl, the most important lessons are often not in perfect speeches, but in the interruptions that try to mess them up."

He gestured with a gentle, giant hand towards Moss, who was happily chewing on a juicy piece of clover, not bothered at all by the morning's drama. "And sometimes," he added, his voice soft with warmth, "the best friends are those who just nudge us towards something new and good."

Holl looked at Moss, his faithful, grounding companion. He looked at Reginald, the mischievous, truth-telling raven. And finally, he looked at Elder Gristle, his wise and compassionate mentor. A deep, warm feeling spread through him, much better than any practiced speech could ever achieve. He did not need to impress with perfect words. He was Holl, and that, he now understood, was more than enough.

"Thank you, Elder Gristle," Holl said, his voice clear and steady, without any fancy words or loud booms. "Truly, thank you for your wisdom."

Reginald the raven, perhaps sensing the profound shift in the atmosphere, let out one last, rather subdued, "Flow of time!" and then, with a powerful beat of his wings, soared off into the bright morning light, his show was over.

Holl, with Moss steadfastly at his side, felt a deep, lasting peace settle over him. He had not delivered his grand speech. But he had learned a lesson of far greater value. And as he shared a quiet, contented breakfast with his mentor, the mountain air seemed to hum with a quiet, special magic. Thus began the real friendship between Ogre Holl and Elder Gristle, started not with big speeches, but with shared laughter about a very persistent, and very helpful, talking raven.
characters: ogre Holl, ram Moss, a goblin innkeeper
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
